reader.title: Killing of a Black child near Fort Smith (1888)
bases: Two drunken men, one of whom fired, shot a four-year-old Black boy on a house porch as they drove past; no mob, band or posse is described, and the two were arrested by a deputy marshal (A1, A5, A2).

A Fort Smith dispatch (A1, A5, A6) and a separately worded Indian Territory brief with different names and details (A2, A3, A10) agree that two drunken men shot and killed a small Black boy at a roadside house.

summary.text: The killing of a Black child near Fort Smith was the fatal shooting of an unnamed boy of about four on the porch of a roadside house about ten miles out of Fort Smith, Arkansas, on the road to the Choctaw Nation, Indian Territory, on April 12, 1888.
One of two drunken men driving home from Fort Smith fired at the boy as they passed, and a deputy marshal arrested both men the same day.
Newspapers across the country reprinted the story as an example of wanton cruelty, and a Fort Smith dispatch called it one of the most horrible murders in the Indian Territory.

According to a Fort Smith dispatch, the two men, named there as Jo Hulsley and J. T. Hunt, left the city in a wagon on a Thursday afternoon for their homes in the Choctaw Nation, with a small boy and a supply of whisky.
They grew boisterous, swinging their pistols and yelling, and about four miles out they frightened a group of children by threatening to shoot them.
About ten miles from town they passed a house where two Black women and a boy of about four sat on the porch.
One of the men said "watch me kill the d—n thing," or words to that effect, and fired; the ball entered the child's back and passed through his body, killing him.
Other versions give the words as "Watch me kill him," "Watch me kill that coon," or "Watch me kill that kid."
The men drove about two miles farther and camped by the road, where Deputy Marshal J. B. Lee found and arrested them at 2 o'clock and took them to jail.

They denied the killing and said a boy traveling with them, who had run off, fired the shot, but officers found no trace of a fourth person, and a pistol was found hidden by the road some distance from the camp.
The boy who had ridden with them was let go.
The dispatch described Hulsley as a son-in-law of the late Choctaw governor Jack McCurtain and "a man of excellent reputation among his people."
No report of an indictment, trial or verdict appears in the coverage.

The Fort Worth Gazette printed the fullest account on April 14 as a special from Fort Smith under the headline "A Horrible Murder," and the same story ran on April 16 in the Washington Evening Star as "A Drunken Man's Murderous Freak" and in the Maysville Evening Bulletin as "Thought It Was Fun."
A Parkersburg weekly ran it as "What Drink Will Do," with "Watch me Shoot That Coon" in the headline, and the Stark County Democrat reprinted the wire on April 19.

A shorter version, which named the men J. T. or J. R. Halsey and J. C. Hulist and called them "two white men," appeared on April 14 in Indianapolis, where the Journal called it a "cold-blooded murder," and in Wilmington.

A German-language Baltimore paper carried a brief on April 16, and a "South and West" column brief ran from April 21 to May 2 in weeklies in Rhode Island, West Virginia, North Carolina and South Carolina.
In the column briefs the story sat without comment among accidents and other crimes.
The versions differ on the men's names, the day, and where the shot struck.
The Fort Smith dispatch gives Thursday and a wound through the back, while the Evening Star's printing says Saturday and the briefs say the bullet went through the breast.
The Fort Smith dispatch, the most detailed and local account, is the better source on names and circumstances; one reprint's "about a mile from town" is probably a slip for ten miles.

accounts.label: Fort Smith dispatch
accounts.gist: Two drunken men driving home to the Choctaw Nation threatened children, then one shot a four-year-old Black boy on a porch ten miles out; a deputy marshal arrested both at their camp.

accounts.label: Accused men's claim
accounts.gist: The two denied the killing and said a boy traveling with them, who had run off, fired the shot; officers found no trace of a fourth party.

accounts.label: Indian Territory brief
accounts.gist: Two white men from Short Mountain, returning drunk from Fort Smith, shot the child after one said 'Watch me kill that coon'; they were arrested and disclaimed the killing.

framing.detail: The Fort Smith special headlined 'A Horrible Murder' and called it 'one of the most horrible that ever occurred in the Indian Territory', while noting Hulsley's 'excellent reputation'.
The Indianapolis Journal called it the 'cold-blooded murder' of a four-year-old boy.
Other papers ran the wire under 'Thought It Was Fun', 'A Drunken Man's Murderous Freak' and 'What Drink Will Do', treating drink as the story.
The 'South and West' column brief ran without comment among accidents and crimes in weekly papers.

Indian Territory (Choctaw Nation), about ten miles from Fort Smith, Ark.; Fort Smith is only where the men set out
Two named men, Hulsey (Halsey) and Hunt (Hulist)
The accused were arrested by Deputy Marshal J. B. Lee and jailed (the victim was never in custody)

info: Thursday afternoon, April 12, 1888 (A1's April 13 dispatch says 'yesterday afternoon'; A5 says 'Thursday'); A6 says 'Saturday afternoon'
At a house by the road about ten miles from Fort Smith, on the way to the Choctaw Nation, Indian Territory (A9 says about a mile from town); A2 and A3 place it near Short Mountain, Indian Territory
An unnamed Black boy about four years old, standing on a porch with two Black women (A1) or in front of a cabin (A3)
Charged with the murder; the men denied the killing and blamed a boy who was with them
Two men, named as Jo Hulsley and J. T. Hunt (A1), J. C. Hulsey and T. J. or J. T. Hunt (A5, A6), or J. T./J. R. Halsey and J. C. Hulist (A2, A3, A10); called 'two white men' in A2 and A10
No report of an indictment, trial or verdict was found
